accuracy.evidence: Checked against the National Curriculum in England English Appendix 1, Years 5 and 6 spelling: words ending in -able and -ible, -ably and -ibly. Its guidance is followed point by point: -able is more common; -able is used when there is a related -ation word (adorable/adoration, applicable/application, considerable/consideration, tolerable/toleration); the e is kept after soft c or g (changeable, noticeable) while forcible and legible take -ible; -able usually follows a complete root (dependable, comfortable, understandable, reasonable, enjoyable, reliable with y to i); -ible is common when no complete root can be heard (possible, horrible, terrible, visible, incredible) but also occurs with one (sensible). Every word in the lab and items was checked against the Appendix examples and standard British and American dictionary spellings (no word differs between them); letter-count items were verified on adore/adorable, notice/noticeable and rely/reliable.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented slips: choosing by ear (step 1 prediction that the endings sound different; challenge dependible and horrable), dropping the e after soft c (step 3 prediction noticable; challenge noticable), keeping an e that should go (adoreable), keeping y (relyable), adding -ly to the whole word (step 5 prediction possiblely; comfortablely, terriblely) and over-applying the guide (step 6 rule breakers sensible, flexible, accessible, capable, probable).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagible is built on the spelling of one suffix pair: a cover-the-ending root test with Whole word / Not a word keys, ending tiles dragged onto a root, a join decision on the root's last letter (keep e, drop e, y to i), a one-letter a-or-i slot that isolates the only difference between the endings, an adverb picker where the e-to-y swap competes with -lely and -ey spellings, and a guide-or-breaker sort. lab_distinct kept it under 30% against flagsfxrule, flagvend, flagunpre, flagmkverb and every other flagship lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner discovers each rule from the feedback on their own choice: picking Whole word for vis returns 'Can you say vis on its own? No, it is only part of a word, so -ible'; drop e for notice returns 'noticable: Keep the e: without it, c before a would sound hard, like cap'; a for forc returns 'forcable would make the c hard'; possiblely returns 'Swap the final e for y'. The done screens list every word built and the step texts confirm the rule afterwards.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions hold a tempting wrong answer the step then disproves: that -able and -ible sound different (the root test step exists because they do not), noticable (the join step shows the e must stay after soft c), and possiblely (the adverb step shows only the e changes). The done line repeats the learner's prediction against the answer.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating questions with twelve distinct wrong-answer messages: whole root given -ible, a made-up -eble ending, partial root given -able, -bel letter order, dropped e after soft c, -ible after a whole root, -ly added to the whole word, -ey ending, y kept before -able, a lost vowel in relible, an e kept in adoreable, and -ible despite an -ation cousin. Every wrong choice in the lab steps gets its own message as well.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs are short with one strategy each and worked examples (Enjoy is a real word, so it is enjoyable. Vis is not a word, so it is visible) and pass the family readability limit; the adult text names the precise terms root word, suffix, unstressed vowel, soft c and g, related -ation word and adverb, within the adult limit. On-canvas instructions are one short line.

no_filler.evidence: The content gate found no banned phrases and the explanation stays under the 12% six-word overlap limit against every lesson, including Suffixes, Suffixes and tricky endings and Converting Words into Verbs. Each hint names the check to make (cover the ending, what sound should the c keep, does the adverb add letters or swap one).

mobile.evidence: Screenshots at 360 px in light and dark for every step, plus mid-step shots after wrong taps: the adverb options overlapped the word tile in the first shot, so the word tile was shrunk and the options moved down with the feedback below them; the drag-an-ending hint was shortened after it was squeezed at 360 px; root, join and vowel keys are at least 56 px tall and sit side by side with 8-12 px gaps.

accessibility.evidence: The browser gate completed every task with Show me on desktop and iPhone 13, the challenge showed, and axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) found no violations in light or dark. Every canvas action has a labelled button (enjoy is a whole word, Add able to break, notice: keep e, Spell it forcible, Spell it comfortably, sensible: Rule breaker) and the canvas aria-label is rewritten with every feedback line. Canvas text is near-black on light tiles in both themes.
